sn35.132:1.3: _Bharataka_ here is unique and its sense debatable. The commentary says they were local householders, but surely the context here is the intrusion of Buddhism into territory dominated by Vedic ritualism. Mahākaccāna was the first major Buddhist figure in the region, and evidently his presence challenged the local brahmins, as the Buddha in the central regions. In the Rig Veda, the Bhāratas were the clan ruled by King Sudās, who, with the blessing of Agni, the “fire of the Bharatas”, and allied with the Vāsiṣṭhas, overcame the armies of ten kings to dominate the Aryan coalition. Wijesekera has argued that _bhara_ in this context originally meant the “booty” or “plunder” gained by raiding villages and towns (*Buddhist and Vedic Studies*, ch. 19). A _bhārata_ was a descendant of the tribe, and with their cultural ascendance became a term for all Vedists. Later it became a general term for “Indians”; the Jain Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra of the 12th century says that Bhāratakas include all Indians, whether Aryan or not (3.29).
sn35.132:6.3: BB has “hypocrisy, bent staffs”, but surely they must be taken together. For all their faults, it seems improbable that they actually upheld hypocrisy as an honorable practice! At Wat Pa Pong, Ajahn Chah used to laugh at those monks who imitated him by carrying a walking stick. Maybe the youths were doing something similar, or it could have been just a general thing. carrying a staff gave an impression of age. Of course, later it became a standard thing for brahmanical ascetics.
